"Coming Out of the Ice: An Unexpected Life" is a memoir by Victor Herman, first published in 1979. The book tells the remarkable and harrowing story of Herman's life, which saw a radical shift from being a Detroit-born American citizen to spending much of his life in the Soviet gulags under oppressive conditions.

Victor Herman moved with his family to the Soviet Union in 1931 when he was a teenager. His father was a tool and die maker from Detroit who was enticed by the prospect of employment in the newly industrializing Soviet Union under Stalin's first five-year plan. However, what seemed like a promising opportunity turned into a nightmare. Although Victor initially thrived in his new environment, becoming a celebrated parachutist and a Soviet sports hero, his situation drastically changed.

In the late 1930s, during the Great Purge, Herman was arrested and falsely accused of espionage. He was then sentenced to spend a decade in one of the notorious Siberian labor camps, where he endured brutal conditions. His memoir details the struggles, both physical and emotional, that he faced while trying to maintain his identity and sanity in such extreme circumstances.

After surviving his sentence, Victor Herman spent many more years in internal exile within the Soviet Union, continuously facing discrimination and hardship. He struggled for years to reclaim his American citizenship and return to the United States, a journey fraught with political and bureaucratic obstacles.

"Coming Out of the Ice" is not just a story of survival against all odds but also a testimony to the resilience of the human spirit. The book also explores themes of political repression, identity, and the impacts of totalitarian regimes on individual lives and freedoms.

In 1982, Herman's experiences were adapted into a television movie, also titled "Coming Out of the Ice," starring John Savage as Herman. This helped bring a wider audience to his extraordinary story. The book and its adaptations shed light on a lesser-known part of history, where personal and geopolitical narratives intersect dramatically. The memoir remains a powerful reminder of the abuses that can occur under authoritarian systems and the dignity and strength required to resist them.
